messages.author: d0bb2cbcd3025fd1
messages.subject: convergence criteria
parts:
Hi all, 

I just came across the package blavaan. It's awesome. Thank you Edgar.  

I am trying to use it for a simulation study in which I want to see whether Bayesian estimation would improve the convergence rate of some models compared to ML estimation. While it is easy to tell whether the model converged, it is more subjective in Bayesian context. I tried the following criteria. But I am not sure whether that is too stringent. 

Basically, what I did is to see whether the largest PSRF in a model is greater 1.1. If it is, then I treated it as evidence of non-convergence. Is this a reasonable choice? Or do you have any better suggestion? 

Additionally, I noted that with 500 observations and 13 variables, it took about 7 hours to finish 100 replications!! I know that Bayesian estimation is very slow. But is this within normal range? 

Thanks a lot. Looking forward to your opinions. 

Best,
Bo

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: convergence criteria
parts:
Bo,

I think the standard recommendation in the literature is to use a PSRF threshold of 1.05. blavaan starts throwing warnings/errors at a PSRF threshold of 1.2 (parameters' posterior means are often stable around this value), but I have found that the newest versions of JAGS and Stan get below 1.05 pretty quickly (for many models, at least). Also, parameters' posterior means tend to be more stable than likelihood values (that go into DIC/WAIC/etc), so I would not assume that the information criteria are stabilized just because the individual parameters have converged.

Regarding speed, that does seem slow. It partly depends on the model, but you might try Stan in addition to JAGS (or vice versa; see the target argument of blavaan). Also, there are some parallelization options that can be sent to JAGS or Stan via the bcontrol argument. Finally, there is also some parallelization built into blavaan that only works on mac/linux machines (for summarizing posterior samples). That parallelization could also theoretically be coded to work on windows, but I currently have no way to do testing on windows.

Best,
Ed

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: convergence criteria
parts:
I would recommend 1.05 because that value has been most established in the literature. Would also be worth looking at the effective sample size of each sampled parameter, which takes autocorrelation into account. (The label is "neff" in the blavaan output.)

Ed

Got you. Thanks.

I have another question. When I tried to use Stan, I got the following message. 

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Warning (non-fatal):
Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
If it does, you need to include a target += statement with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
Left-hand-side of sampling statement:
    etaUNC ~ sem_lv_lpdf(...)



Then later, I got a lot of the following errors. 

Rejecting initial value:
  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.
Exception: cholesky_decompose: Matrix m is not positive definite  (in 'modela8ce29547e1b_202c686dfbc70d982b3ce715a1537917' at line 249)


Do you have any idea what's going on? When I use JAGS, the model ran smoothly. 

Thanks,
Bo

(Could send to my email if you want, as opposed to the whole group.)

Ed

I am trying to use it for a simulation study in which I want to see whether Bayesian estimation would improve the convergence rate of some models compared to ML estimation. While it is easy to tell whether the model converged, it is more subjective in Bayesian context. I tried the following criteria. But I am not sure whether that is too stringent. 

Basically, what I did is to see whether the largest PSRF in a model is greater 1.1. If it is, then I treated it as evidence of non-convergence. Is this a reasonable choice? Or do you have any better suggestion? 

Additionally, I noted that with 500 observations and 13 variables, it took about 7 hours to finish 100 replications!! I know that Bayesian estimation is very slow. But is this within normal range? 

Thanks a lot. Looking forward to your opinions. 

Best,
Bo

Got you. Thanks.

I have another question. When I tried to use Stan, I got the following message. 

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Warning (non-fatal):
Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
If it does, you need to include a target += statement with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
Left-hand-side of sampling statement:

Then later, I got a lot of the following errors. 

Rejecting initial value:
  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.
Exception: cholesky_decompose: Matrix m is not positive definite  (in 'modela8ce29547e1b_202c686dfbc70d982b3ce715a1537917' at line 249)


Do you have any idea what's going on? When I use JAGS, the model ran smoothly. 

Thanks,
Bo

On Wednesday, June 27, 2018 at 2:46:35 PM UTC-5, Ed Merkle wrote:
I would recommend 1.05 because that value has been most established in the literature. Would also be worth looking at the effective sample size of each sampled parameter, which takes autocorrelation into account. (The label is "neff" in the blavaan output.)

Ed

On Wed, Jun 27, 2018 at 1:02 PM, Bo <bobby1...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Edgar, 

Thanks for your prompt reply. 

Given my research questions, then what do you recommend as cutoff for convergence? 

Regarding speed, I was using JAGS. I will try Stan accompanied by parallel computing. 

Thanks again.

Best,
Bo

On Wednesday, June 27, 2018 at 12:42:16 PM UTC-5, Ed Merkle wrote:
Bo,

I think the standard recommendation in the literature is to use a PSRF threshold of 1.05. blavaan starts throwing warnings/errors at a PSRF threshold of 1.2 (parameters' posterior means are often stable around this value), but I have found that the newest versions of JAGS and Stan get below 1.05 pretty quickly (for many models, at least). Also, parameters' posterior means tend to be more stable than likelihood values (that go into DIC/WAIC/etc), so I would not assume that the information criteria are stabilized just because the individual parameters have converged.

Regarding speed, that does seem slow. It partly depends on the model, but you might try Stan in addition to JAGS (or vice versa; see the target argument of blavaan). Also, there are some parallelization options that can be sent to JAGS or Stan via the bcontrol argument. Finally, there is also some parallelization built into blavaan that only works on mac/linux machines (for summarizing posterior samples). That parallelization could also theoretically be coded to work on windows, but I currently have no way to do testing on windows.

Best,
Ed

parts:
Actually, I cannot immediately find a reference to that value. I think it is the default that runjags uses for automatic convergence assessment, and I know that some reviewers have talked about that value. Also, sometimes people talk about a threshold on the upper bound of a confidence interval for Rhat, as opposed to a threshold on the computed value of Rhat. But I could be incorrect on the 1.05 value.

Ed
